stem:
Veena has a triangle with a right angle at $C$, and side lengths $a=BC$, $b=AC$, and $c=AB$.

Which claim applies $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ correctly?

options.text: Write $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ for the side lengths even when angle $C$ is not a right angle.
Say that writing $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ is what creates the right angle at $C$, instead of using the right angle to name the hypotenuse.
Because $\angle C=90^{\circ}$, the hypotenuse is $AB=c$ opposite $C$, so $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$.
Also apply $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ unchanged to every acute triangle with sides $a$, $b$, and $c$, beyond right-angled triangles.

teacher.key_rationale: Pythagoras needs a right angle: the hypotenuse is opposite that angle, so $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$ with $c=AB$. Dropping the right-angle condition, reversing equation and right angle, or stretching to acute triangles all miss that hinge.
